item.title: Chris Rock says President Trump is correct on one key issue, and it almost redeems his ‘other sins’
item.description: Chris Rock says Trump got it right about fake news, calling media bias the one thing that "almost" clears Trump of all his "other sins" in a new interview.
item.content:encoded:
Legendary actor and comedian Chris Rock argued that, if nothing else, President Donald Trump is dead-on accurate when criticizing the news as "fake."

Rock spoke to Variety about his upcoming film, "Misty Green," offering candid commentary on the entertainment industry. During the interview, Variety noted that Rock still has the same "opinionated, incendiary persona that caught Eddie Murphy’s eye at a New York comedy club one night when Rock was just 19."

"Rock was one of the few celebrities to publicly predict Donald Trump would win the 2016 election," Variety wrote. "And speaking about the president today, Rock says, ‘I’m not a fan. But it’s weird when somebody gets one thing right, and the one thing almost clears them of all their other sins. The news is fake. He got that right.’"

Curtis Houck, managing editor of the Media Research Center's NewsBusters, responded to Rock's comments in a statement to Fox News Digital.

EX-CNN ANCHOR DON LEMON AGREES TRUMP PLAYED LIBERAL NETWORK 'LIKE PUPPETS'

"In this day and age, we often find ourselves feeling like we’re approaching cats-and-dogs living together on certain issues, and that includes the acknowledgment that the legacy, elitist media have failed to serve the public," Houck said. 

"The widespread awareness of both media bias and press ineptitude will be one of President Trump’s longest-lasting legacies. Chris Rock certainly seems to be on the president’s wavelength."

In 2023, Rock raised eyebrows by warning U.S. lawmakers that arresting Trump would only make him "more popular."

Rock had made the comments while in Washington, D.C., for an event honoring Adam Sandler. He began poking fun at the well-connected crowd, which included former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and members of President Biden's administration.

CRAIG FERGUSON REVEALS WHY TRUMP JOKES ARE MISSING FROM HIS NEW COMEDY TOUR

"Are you guys really going to arrest Trump?" Rock asked. "Do you know this is only going to make him more popular. It's like arresting Tupac. He's just gonna sell more records. Are you stupid?" 

Fox News Digital's Anders Hagstrom contributed to this report.

item.title: The potential replacement for Dabo Swinney at Clemson is staring the Tigers right in the face
item.description: Tony Elliott's historic run at Virginia makes the Clemson Tigers alum and former coordinator the obvious choice if the Dabo Swinney era ends.
item.content:encoded:
If you've been paying attention at all, you know the Clemson Tigers are at a bit of a crossroads.

Even casual college football fans can see the writing on the wall, as the once-proud national powerhouse has fallen on hard times, culminating in a 51-10 beatdown at the hands of LSU on Saturday night.

I've written a lot about Tigers head coach Dabo Swinney and the thin line between respecting his past accomplishments and ushering the program into the NIL era, but lately I've found myself wondering if he's used up his nine lives.

HOW MUCH LONGER DOES CLEMSON HEAD COACH DABO SWINNEY REALISTICALLY HAVE IN DEATH VALLEY?

Saturday wasn't anything new - Clemson getting clobbered by a quality opponent has happened quite often post-Covid – but the fact that the general public has changed its reaction to the ritualistic sacrifices from shock to apathy shows that the Tigers aren't what they used to be.

And that starts at the top.

It's probably not a hot take to say that it's time for Clemson to make a change at head coach.

The game appears to be passing Dabo by at warp speed, and although he won the ACC and made the College Football Playoff just two seasons ago, the conference is only getting tougher, and opponents like Miam, which used to be stepping stones for the Tigers on their way to a championship, are now leaning into the "new model" and lapping the old rulers of the realm.

But getting rid of a coach is only half of the equation, and the question still remains: Who does Clemson replace Swinney with should it choose to move on from him?

The Tigers are one of the few "haves" in a world of "have nots," meaning they could pick from a list of elite head coaches and not have to go too far down before hearing a "yes."

However, going "big game hunting" isn't always the answer.

Texas A&M, LSU, and USC are all some of the biggest brands in college football, and when they were in the market for a head coach, all three went after names who were "too big to fail."

The Aggies secured Jimbo Fisher, who had won a national championship at Florida State less than half a decade ago.

The Tigers and Trojans were searching for a new head coach during the same hiring cycle, and both came away with options that were deemed absolute coups at the time in Brian Kelly and Lincoln Riley, respectively.

Today, only one of those three coaches is still employed by the last school to hire him, as Fisher and Kelly both failed to live up to the lofty expectations placed upon them when they arrived on campus.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Riley is still plugging away at USC, and although things seem to be trending up in Los Angeles, he's in year five without a single Playoff appearance to show so far, hardly the type of tenure any Trojans fan would have envisioned when they plucked him from Oklahoma in late 2021.

All that is to say, Clemson doesn't need to hire the "sexy name" to have a successful coaching search. They need to hire the right guy.

And I believe the answer is staring the Tigers right in the face.

If Clemson pulls the plug on the Dabo Swinney era, its first call should be to Tony Elliott at Virginia.

Elliott is fairly young for a head coach at only 46 years old, and he has the Cavaliers trending in a historic direction.

After increasing Virginia's conference win totals every season since arriving in Charlottesville, Elliott guided the Cavs to an 11-win season and an ACC title game berth.

Those 11 wins were the most in school history, and the up-and-coming head coach was awarded the Paul "Bear" Bryant Coach of the Year award for his efforts.

He has the Cavaliers ranked in the AP Top-25 again this season after a rout of NC State in week zero, a team many thought would be a darkhorse contender in the ACC.

It doesn't take a rocket scientist to see that Clemson has far more resources and deeper pockets for football than Virginia.

If he's doing this well with the Cavaliers in the same conference, imagine what Elliott could do with the Tigers.

But it's not just his coaching acumen that should have him at the top of the list.

Because Tony Elliott is also a Clemson alum.

He played for the Tigers in the early 2000s, and in addition to that, he was the offensive coordinator under Swinney for seven seasons, helping his alma mater win two national championships in the process.

The idea of having an alum coach his school is becoming increasingly popular, particularly in the ACC.

Brent Key (Georgia Tech), Jeff Brohm (Louisville), and Mario Cristobal (Miami) are all coaching at the schools they played for, and experiencing great success in the process.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Elliot is crushing the previous baseline established at Virginia, he will be a hot name in any coaching search for the next few seasons, and he's a former player and coordinator with the Tigers.

Let's not overthink this, Clemson.

Dabo's replacement is there for the taking, just make the call.

item.title: Spanish opposition leader calls prime minister a ‘traitor’ over Ceuta migrant crisis
item.description: Santiago Abascal branded Pedro Sánchez a "traitor" in parliament over Spain's migrant crisis in the North African enclave of Ceuta amid protests.
item.content:encoded:
A Spanish opposition leader branded the country's socialist prime minister a traitor over his government's handling of the influx of migrants in a North African enclave.

Santiago Abascal, leader of the Vox party, spoke during a parliamentary session when he asked if Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez was being blackmailed by Morocco amid the border crisis in Ceuta.

During his remarks, Abascal called Sánchez a "traitor" and "a dog."

FIREBRAND REP UNLOADS ON SOCIALIST PRIME MINISTER AS 'HORDES OF MILITARY AGED MEN' SWARM EUROPEAN COUNTRY

Sánchez responded in a heated back-and-forth, saying, "I may be a dog, but I have no master."

Abascal then held up sheets of paper one by one that spelled out "Traidor," Spanish for "Traitor." Sánchez then sat down.

Spain has seen major protests in response to the migrant arrivals in Ceuta, with critics blaming Sánchez for the crisis and some accusing him of pandering to Morocco.

LOCALS TORCH MIGRANT SHELTERS AS SPAIN'S PM POINTS BLAME BEYOND THE BORDER

More than 70,000 migrants poured into Ceuta in July. Most of them have returned to Morocco, but many remain in the enclave, with some living in tent encampments on the beach.

Meanwhile, Spain’s national intelligence agency issued multiple warnings before the mass crossing of migrants from Morocco into Ceuta in late July, according to declassified documents released by the government on Wednesday, The Associated Press reported.

"There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers," the declassified WhatsApp message said, "just to give you an idea of its scale."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Caitlyn Jenner says she may enter the WNBA Draft to challenge trans athlete eligibility rules
item.description: Caitlyn Jenner said she told Enes Kanter Freedom she might sign up for the 2027 WNBA Draft as a "real trans person" to challenge eligibility rules.
item.content:encoded:
As Enes Kanter Freedom continues to challenge the eligibility rules of the WNBA, someone else may be tempted to do the same.

Caitlyn Jenner, who Freedom has mentioned in his "peace summit" idea to talk with WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert and the WNBA task force about the eligibility controversy, mentioned on "Planet Tyrus" that she has spoken with Freedom on multiple occasions.

During one of them, Jenner admitted she, as a "real trans person," told Freedom she might even consider entering the WNBA draft.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Enes and I have talked on the phone quite a few times, and I even told him one time — this is a couple of weeks ago — ‘Enes, I’m like a real trans person. Maybe I should sign up for the 2027 WNBA draft,’" Jenner told Tyrus.

Jenner went on to mention that, back in the 1970s while becoming an American athletic icon as Bruce Jenner following a record-breaking decathlon gold medal at the 1976 Summer Olympics in Montreal, she was drafted by the then-Kansas City Kings in the NBA.

These are the same Kings which now play in Sacramento following an original stint in Kansas City from 1972-85. While Jenner played basketball growing up, it was the decathlon she gave her undivided attention.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Still, the basketball skill is there, and Jenner is one of the most well-known trans persons in the country. Would the WNBA step in if the 76-year-old entered the draft?

"All the WNBA had to say was, ‘You can’t play in our league because you are a man. This is a woman’s league.’ That’s it, it’s over. News cycle’s done," Tyrus said earlier in their hour-long conversation.

"Maybe they don’t want the news cycle being done," Jenner responded. "Yes, that’s a good point."

"Well, look at Sophie Cunningham and what happened with her — the WNBA has never got so much press."

Late last month, Freedom posted a video on X following his ejection from Wintrust Arena after a spat with Chicago Sky guard Natasha Cloud in a game where they played Cunningham and the Indiana Fever. Freedom was speaking directly to Engelbert and the WNBA task force in his video, where he mentioned Jenner could moderate the "peace summit."

"I’ve already spoken with her, and she’s in," Freedom wrote on X. "…Listen, the whole world is laughing at you. You have turned the #WNBA into a laughingstock. It’s time to stop hiding behind closed-door meetings, excuses, and delays and finally give the public a clear answer. Let’s have a peace summit. No shouting. No hiding. No carefully scripted statements.

CAITLYN JENNER SAYS THERE'S A 'SIMPLE' SOLUTION TO END THE WNBA'S TRANS ATHLETE DEBATE

"Let’s sit across the table from each other, have an open and respectful conversation, and address the questions millions of people are asking."

Engelbert and the league have not responded to Freedom, whom referenced the WNBA task force that came to no decision of what justified a woman while deliberating over eligibility concerns in a recent meeting.

Jenner has long been an advocate for keeping biological men out of women’s sports. She has even given her "simple" solution to end the WNBA’s trans athlete debate amid Freedom and Royce White’s endeavors.

"They’re showing the hypocrisy of what’s going on out there in the WNBA," Jenner said of Kanter and White on "Fox News @ Night" with Trace Gallagher . "The WNBA had their meetings on this issue and Cathy (Engelbert), the head, says, ‘We talked about the trans issue but we just haven’t come up with a conclusion at this point. We will continue the conversation.’ Cathy, XX, you’re in. XY you’re out. It’s that simple.

"And both these guys I think are doing a good job just to show the WNBA the hypocrisy that’s going on here. We have to protect women’s sports … I want to protect women’s sports. Title IX was one of the greatest legislations for women’s equality – that happened to be in sports."

item.title: Tyler Herro's model girlfriend hits free agency after his trade to Milwaukee, court docs reveal
item.description: Tyler Herro and Katya Elise Henry are duking it out in court over custody and support after nearly seven years together, according to court documents.
item.content:encoded:
It seems like just yesterday that I was documenting Tyler Herro's Instagram model girlfriend Katya Elise Henry's battle through something she called "Project Booty Challenge." The reality is that it's been almost three years.

A lot can and has changed in that amount of time. Back then, they had just put an apparent breakup and cheating rumors behind them. Herro was four years into his NBA career and they had a growing family.

Fast-forward to June and Herro found himself in a blockbuster trade that sent Giannis Antetokounmpo from the Milwaukee Bucks to the Miami Heat. He was headed back home to Wisconsin, but would his model girlfriend be joining him?

FORMER HEAT TEAMMATES BAM ADEBAYO, TYLER HERRO INVOLVED IN HEATED LAS VEGAS EXCHANGE: REPORT

The answer to that question appears to have arrived on Tuesday in the form of court documents obtained by TMZ. According to the docs, Herro and Henry have called it quits and are "duking it out in court over custody and support."

They've both reportedly filed lawsuits. However, the Bucks guard is said to have dismissed his case days later. He had asked the court to set up a parenting schedule and determine the amount of child support he should be paying.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

He claims to have been paying her support voluntarily since she gave birth. For her part, Henry says in her filing that she was in a relationship with Herro for almost 7 years and that she was the primary caregiver for their two children.

She's asking for primary custody and wants their children to see their dad with "safeguards and parameters" in place. She reportedly cited "historical conduct" that she purposefully left out of her filing out of respect.

Things move quickly in the NBA. One minute you're a star living it up in a city like Miami and the next you're being packaged up in a deal for a bigger star and shipped off to Milwaukee.

I'm not going to pretend to know why these two called it quits and if the trade played any sort of significant role in their split. I will go out on a limb and say that it didn't help.

item.title: ESPN hopes to make Peter Schrager its first homegrown star in over a decade | Bobby Burack
item.description: Peter Schrager joins Pat McAfee and Stephen A. Smith as ESPN personalities with shows built around them, but key concerns loom over his path.
item.content:encoded:
If you speak to anyone in or around ESPN, they will tell you the same story about Peter Schrager: ESPN wants him to be its next big star.

On Thursday, the network will debut "Big Day with Peter Schrager." The program will air weekdays at 2 p.m., as OutKick first reported in July.

Schrager joins a short list of individuals with ESPN television shows in 2026 built specifically around their personality. Pat McAfee, Stephen A. Smith, Mike Greenberg and Scott Van Pelt are the others. That group should tell you all you need to know about how the network views Schrager.

HERE IS HOW PAT MCAFEE HAS SURPASSED STEPHEN A SMITH AS THE FACE OF ESPN | BOBBY BURACK

Schrager will also be the first personality under Burke Magnus’ regime to receive a push toward potential stardom. Remember, ESPN did not make McAfee a star. He was already a star before signing with the network. In fact, ESPN licensed McAfee’s show to a then-record-setting deal because it had so mightily struggled to create new stars in-house.

McAfee had leverage because none of the personalities ESPN previously tried to establish had any. That list includes Bomani Jones, Sarah Spain, Katie Nolan, Monica McNutt, Jemele Hill, Michael Smith and Mina Kimes.

Schrager represents a change of pace from that group. He fits ESPN’s preferred direction of leaning into the positivity and excitement surrounding sports, rather than the negative and polarizing coverage that had become standard.

Last month, ESPN executive Mike Foss emphasized during a town hall the company’s desire to move away from "hot takes."

Schrager also provides more expertise than other personalities ESPN hoped to brand around. He has a background in NFL reporting. He is more knowledgeable than those who cover the league primarily through the lens of the culture war.

On the surface, Schrager’s prospects are promising. But concerns remain. One involves the executive who hired and elevated him.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Last week, OutKick explained how Magnus undermined his own edict and vision by hiring back Stan Verrett to host a throwaway show on NFL Network. During his first tenure, Verrett represented the very type of behavior Magnus had spent the past few years weeding out, including deranged posts, unprofessional direct messages to reporters, and preposterous race talk.

We believe Magnus felt pressure after Ryan Clark name-dropped him in unfounded accusations of racism following Clark’s firing. ESPN did not deny our understanding of Magnus’ position.

If Magnus has set out to prove that he is not a racist, he could derail Schrager’s new show by surrounding him with polarizing individuals eager to impress their audiences on Threads, Bluesky, and Black Twitter.

This is an issue elsewhere at the company. Nearly every ESPN program features a rotating cast of panelists, most of whom viewers are not tuning in to hear. Get Up is now more about Chris Canty and Chiney Ogwumike than Greenberg, one of the last few difference-makers left at the company.

Schrager has not shown that he has the chops to push back against said hysteria. During Super Bowl week, he nodded along on set as NFL defensive lineman Cam Jordan spewed nonsense in an effort to argue that Lamar Jackson is a better postseason quarterback than Josh Allen, despite all evidence to the contrary.

That was a bad look for Schrager. He looked scared.

WHY DID BURKE MAGNUS HIRE BACK STAN VERRETT?

Therefore, the question begs whether Schrager is prepared to push back when, say, McNutt and David Dennis Jr. belittle and downplay Caitlin Clark while further advancing racial narratives. Whether he is could swiftly determine the success and perception of his program.

There is a reason NFL Live is growing at double-digit rates while First Take is stagnant. Sports fans want fun, not polarization. We thought Magnus understood that. The hiring of Verrett casts doubt on whether he does.

Finally, while live sports and streaming will ultimately define ESPN’s success, it is important that the network casts Schrager right.

Most of the company’s biggest stars are around 60 years old, including Stephen A., Greenberg and Van Pelt. At 44, Schrager could have a long runway alongside McAfee, who is 39.

Laura Rutledge, 37, Josh Pate, 40, and Malika Andrews, 31, are other potential future stars for the network.

If there were ever a sports personality we would strongly advise to stick to sports and stay off X, it would be Peter Schrager. He has the chance and talents to become one of the faces of ESPN for the next decade.

But ESPN hasn't built a star on its own since Stephen A. Smith. That was in 2015. Schrager will have to buck that trend.

item.title: Dolly Parton 'could not bear negative things' and kept her cancer diagnosis from fans and family
item.description: Stella Parton reveals that Dolly Parton kept her cancer diagnosis secret because she "did not want people sad" or her fans and family worried.
item.content:encoded:
Dolly Parton's sister is sharing why the legendary singer kept her cancer diagnosis a secret.

In an interview with "CBS Mornings'" scheduled to air Thursday, Sept. 10, her sister, Stella Parton, said Dolly didn't go public with her cancer diagnosis because she "did not want people sad," revealing she didn't even share the news with her entire family.

"Well, Dolly did not want anybody to tell that, because Dolly could not bear negative things, and she would not have wanted her fans worried about it," she shared. "She didn’t want a lot of the family worried about it. Some of us knew, the ones that were closer, but not every relative."

The "Jolene" singer died at the age of 80 Aug. 25 after a "brief battle with cancer."

DOLLY PARTON OFFERED TO TRY EXPERIMENTAL DRUGS IF ‘NO HOPE’ FOR CANCER BATTLE TO HELP OTHERS, SISTER SAYS

News of her death was announced on her Instagram by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, in which he highlighted her body of work as a musician, as well as her philanthropic work with the Imagination Library.

Her death inspired tributes on social media from fans around the world, including musicians and actors, something Stella says the "9 to 5" star would have been happy with.

"She’d be really happy and delighted that people have shown her so much love because she knew that that would make us feel better as her family," Stella said. "Bottom line, end of the day, her family and Carl’s family and probably Judy’s family are the people that she would want to say, ‘See, everything I did, they cared. They really loved me."

Dolly rose to stardom in 1967 when she began appearing on "The Porter Wagoner Show." During her time on the show, the two released many iconic duets and were nominated for many Grammys together.

She chose to leave the show and focus on her solo career in 1974, after seven years with the program.

In an effort to explain to Wagoner, who had become her close friend during her tenure on the show and was unhappy with the news, why she needed to leave the show, she wrote one of her biggest hits, "I Will Always Love You."

"I sang the song alone in his office — just me and my guitar," she told Howard Stern in 2023, adding that he replied, "That’s the best song you’ve ever wrote … You can go if I can produce the song."

She won 10 Grammy Awards, received a Kennedy Center Honor, got a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, Country Music Hall of Fame and Songwriters Hall of Fame.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

In addition to her success as a country music star, Dolly was also a philanthropist. She launched the Imagination Library, a book gifting program which sends one book a month to children across the country regardless of their family's economic status.

"When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true," Dolly said in a statement on the organization's website. "I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister.

"Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer," she continued. "The seeds of these dreams are often found in books, and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world."

item.title: Surrogate who refused abortion takes fight to Supreme Court as baby's life hangs in balance
item.description: Surrogate McKenna West asks the Supreme Court to block a California ruling that left her unable to advocate for a newborn with a rare heart defect.
item.content:encoded:
A surrogate who defied a California couple’s demand to abort their baby after a devastating heart diagnosis is taking her fight to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing a lower court ruling has left her powerless to advocate for the medically fragile newborn.

Attorneys for Alaska cardiac nurse McKenna West filed an emergency application Wednesday, asking Justice Elena Kagan to temporarily block a Los Angeles court ruling that declared the California couple the baby’s legal parents.

Kagan handles emergency matters arising from the 9th Circuit, which includes California. She has not ruled on the request.

SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION

West carried the child under a surrogacy agreement with California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed, who call the baby Rumi. West calls him Gabriel.

The baby was born in Texas Aug. 12 with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, or HLHS, a rare condition in which the left side of the heart is severely underdeveloped.

KAGAN RECALLS LINDSEY GRAHAM'S VOTE THAT HELPED SEAL HER SUPREME COURT CONFIRMATION

The legal war began after the condition was detected during a 20-week ultrasound. West alleges Gilkar and Ahmed asked her to terminate the pregnancy under a provision in their surrogacy agreement covering serious fetal abnormalities.

West refused, telling the surrogacy agency she could not abort "this precious baby" after feeling him move and learning treatment was available, according to the filing.

She offered to raise the child herself or arrange an adoption if the couple no longer wanted him, while allowing them to walk away from any further financial obligations.

Her attorneys allege West was then warned that continuing the pregnancy could expose her to more than $250,000 in financial penalties.

CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION

Gilkar and Ahmed later turned to a California court to establish their legal rights as the baby’s parents. West argued the case belonged in Alaska under the surrogacy agreement and said she appeared in California solely to challenge the court’s jurisdiction.

The Los Angeles Superior Court determined that West had effectively consented to its authority by submitting a 147-page filing that addressed the "substance of the issues," according to the application.

West’s lawyers said most of those pages were exhibits supporting her jurisdictional challenge and that she had repeatedly refused to argue the underlying case.

"Any reasonable view of consent would recognize that ‘no’ does not mean ‘yes,’" they wrote.

West also claims she was never properly served. Her filing says a FedEx package containing the court papers was delivered to her babysitter, who allegedly was not told what was inside.

The California court declared Gilkar and Ahmed the baby’s legal parents June 22, and West failed to persuade three state courts to put the ruling on hold.

SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION

The judge acknowledged during the California proceedings that the dispute "[m]ay be a question of life and death" for the unborn child, according to West’s application.

The fight then moved to Texas, where West traveled so the baby could be delivered at a hospital equipped to treat his condition.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured an emergency order before the birth, directing the hospital to provide life-saving care and preventing the child from being removed from the state.

West previously said she had only about one minute with the newborn while his umbilical cord was still attached before he was taken from her. A court order later barred her from seeing or holding him.

The baby underwent the first of three anticipated open-heart surgeries Aug. 17. He was later returned to a breathing tube after his condition declined, according to court filings previously reviewed by Fox News Digital.

Gilkar said during a hearing last month in Dallas that the couple had remained at their son’s bedside and accused West of trying to take him.

"He’s our child," Gilkar said, according to The Associated Press. "He’s the love of our lives."

She also told the court the newborn was "suffering a lot" as he struggled to breathe, choked on tubes and required a blood transfusion following surgery, according to the AP.

West has said she would abandon her custody effort if a court determined the intended parents were committed to providing the child with life-saving care.

But on Sept. 2, a Texas judge upheld the California ruling and removed West from the case. Paxton has also stepped away from the legal fight.

HHS WARNS TEXAS HOSPITALS AGAINST DENYING LIFE-SAVING CARE TO NEWBORN WITH DISABILITY

West’s attorneys argue she is now barred from receiving information about the baby or defending the order requiring his continued treatment. They allege Gilkar and Ahmed are challenging that medical care order.

The couple previously agreed to the baby’s first surgery and said they would approve life-saving care if doctors determined he was a candidate.

West is now asking the Supreme Court to temporarily block the California ruling, which could give her a path back into the Texas case. Her attorneys argue the dispute raises a broader constitutional question over whether challenging a court’s authority can itself be treated as accepting that authority.

Her lawyers stressed that temporarily blocking the ruling would not decide who the baby’s legal parents are or direct doctors to provide a particular course of treatment. Instead, it could allow West to ask the Texas court to bring her back into the case.

Without Supreme Court intervention, her attorneys warned, West will remain shut out of decisions and updates about the baby’s condition as the appeals process plays out.

"Unless this Court provides relief from that judgment, M.W. will have no access to information about Baby G.’s condition," West’s attorneys wrote.

They argued that a victory later could come too late to protect the child.

"Relief later in Texas proceedings may only restore her right to protect a child that has already passed," the filing states.

Fox News’ Shannon Bream and Bill Mears contributed to this report.

item.title: Potential Dem presidential contender crashes GOP convention, tries to snatch spotlight from Trump
item.description: Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker claims Republicans are trying to "rig" the 2026 midterm elections as the GOP kicks off its first-ever convention in Dallas.
item.content:encoded:
DALLAS — Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois is urging voters to ignore the Republicans' first-ever midterm convention.

"Voters can see through the BS that Republicans are spewing," Pritzker told reporters at a Democratic National Committee-hosted counter programming news conference across the street from the American Airlines Center in Dallas, the site of this week’s first-ever Republican midterm convention.

With less than two months until the midterm elections — and early voting just weeks away — President Donald Trump and the GOP kicked off their convention Wednesday as Republicans fight to keep control of Congress.

The GOP's playbook for the convention, which comes as Republicans face energized Democrats and political headwinds as they defend their slim House and Senate majorities, is to motivate the party's base and boost turnout in key races that will determine control of Congress.

GOP MIDTERM CONVENTION: CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN?

"We are putting the president on the ballot," Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters emphasized in a Fox News Digital interview on the eve of the gathering. "That's exactly what we're doing with this midterm convention."

But Pritzker, a potential 2028 White House contender, blasted the two-day GOP confab.

"This bizarre Republican midterm convention here can't paper over the fact that Republicans have done nothing to earn your vote," Pritzker said. 

"Donald Trump is hoping that a flashy primetime event will make you forget that, well, his trade war is killing costs for families at the grocery store. His war in Iran is killing ranchers and farmers and their way of life, and his war on people, on the working people, the working families of this country are raising the costs of health care and housing."

FIRST ON FOX: WHO'S SPEAKING — AND WHEN — AT THE GOP'S HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION

The governor also charged that Republicans are trying to "rig" the midterm elections, arguing that Trump is aiming to use the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail-in balloting across the country.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

item.title: Manhattan prostitute pleads guilty to killing 3 men with fentanyl-laced drugs in robbery scheme
item.description: Tabitha Bundrick admitted to feeding fentanyl-laced drugs to three men during encounters across Manhattan, then robbing them as they lay unconscious.
item.content:encoded:
headlines

A Manhattan prostitute who killed three johns when she fed them fentanyl-laced drugs to rob them pleaded guilty Tuesday.

Tabitha Bundrick, 39, admitted to giving her customers the powerful synthetic opioid between April 2023 and February 2024 and then taking their personal belongings, including their cell phones, sneakers, money and watches, the Manhattan District Attorney's Office said.

"The defendant knowingly killed three people by providing them fentanyl-laced drugs," said District Attorney Alvin Bragg. "As they lay unconscious, she robbed her victims and left them to die. In several instances, the victims’ bodies were found by their friends or family members."

FENTANYL DEATHS COULD NOW COST DRUG DEALERS THEIR LIVES UNDER NEW GOP PROPOSAL

Bundrick showed a "shocking indifference" to the lives of her victims, Bragg said.

She is expected to be sentenced to 27 years to life for three counts of second-degree murder and one count of second-degree assault.

Bundrick's crimes began on April 30, 2023, when she met Mario Paullan, 42, and his friend on the street and offered to sell them soap. She then offered to have sex with them for money and took them to an apartment she broke into, prosecutors said.

NEW YORK BODEGA WORKER KILLED LESS THAN A YEAR AFTER EXPRESSING FEAR TO REPORTER OVER VIOLENCE

After taking the fentanyl-laced drugs she gave them, Paullan's friend woke up to find him dead the next morning and their belongings missing, authorities said.

Months later, she met Miguel Navez, 39, and gave him drugs at his apartment. He was found three days later by his brother, with his belongings also stolen.

The third incident occurred on Feb. 25, 2024, when Abrihan Fernandez, 34, died in his apartment. Bundrick was caught entering and exiting the Upper Manhattan apartment several times with large bags.

She is scheduled to be sentenced on Oct. 6.

item.title: Gavin Newsom expresses 'openness' to packing SCOTUS, calls Electoral College system 'perverted'
item.description: Dem California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he was "evolving" on the idea of expanding the Supreme Court and eliminating the Electoral College during an interview Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed "openness" to reforming the Supreme Court and claimed the Electoral College "perverted" politics during an interview with former CNN host Don Lemon on his podcast Tuesday.

Near the end of the interview, Lemon directly asked Newsom, a rumored 2028 candidate, whether he believed the judicial branch needed to be expanded, an idea pushed by several Democratic figures, including former Vice President Kamala Harris.

"My initial instinct — me, a year ago, I would have said no out of concern that it will continue to be expanded," Newsom said. 

"And I was making a case for the ethical reforms and term limits, 18 years, which I was making a case a year ago. I'm more open to it on the basis of those district court arguments, which are not terrible arguments."

DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION

"Is that a yes?" Lemon asked.

"I'm finding myself evolving on it. I normally have very clear conviction on things. I've been open to argument and interested in the evidence on this," Newsom answered.

He described his position as "caution on expanding it, but openness," adding that he believes reforms like term limits are a "no-brainer."

HARRIS LABELED 'INSTITUTIONAL ARSONIST' FOR PLAN TO FUNDAMENTALLY TRANSFORM SCOTUS AND ELECTORAL COLLEGE

The California Democrat had harsher criticism of the Electoral College, suggesting that it has "perverted" U.S. politics.

"California has already been a leader that's already gone out front saying it's time to change that system. Which state's more burdened by it than my state? We're the size of 21 state populations combined. Come on. And we have two representatives in the Senate? Come on. 

"And the way that thing favors ... it's perverted, I think, our politics. The Constitution is a living document, and it was conceived to be amended, and I think it's time to make that amendment," Newsom said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

CARVILLE TELLS DEMS TO QUIETLY PREPARE POWER GRAB WITH DC, PUERTO RICO STATEHOOD AND SUPREME COURT PACKING

Though Newsom has not explicitly supported expanding the Supreme Court, he made similar comments suggesting an openness to it during an interview with Brian Tyler Cohen on his podcast in June. Cohen was arguing in favor of court expansion, and Newsom remarked that Cohen was "getting me closer to your point of view."

During an interview with "PBS NewsHour" on Monday, Newsom also said the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) on issues like universal healthcare, climate change and moving off fossil fuels. The DSA's goals include eliminating the Supreme Court and replacing it with a judiciary that would be selected by Congress.

House Democrats recently voted against a constitutional amendment to cap the number of justices on the Supreme Court at nine. Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., who introduced the measure, warned Congress about the downsides of expanding the court.

"Here's the question every American should ask: If a sitting majority can change the size of the Supreme Court the moment it dislikes rulings, what happens to the next time the other side is in power?" Biggs said on the floor.

item.title: Beauty school moms caught in accreditation crossfire as Trump administration weighs consequential decision
item.description: Trump's Department of Education faces a pivotal decision on NACCAS accreditation that could cut federal student aid for 120,000 beauty students.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration is weighing the future of an accreditor overseeing roughly 1,300 beauty and cosmetology schools and more than 120,000 students, in a decision that could test how the president’s push to overhaul higher education accreditation is applied beyond the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) battles that have dominated the issue.

President Donald Trump promised during the 2024 campaign to "fire the radical left accreditors" and called accreditation his "secret weapon" against colleges and universities he argued had been captured by the political left.

But the case now before the U.S. Department of Education (DOE) is different.

Rather than allegations involving DEI requirements, it centers on whether the National Accrediting Commission of Career Arts and Sciences, or NACCAS, has complied with federal requirements and what consequences should follow if it has not.

MCMAHON TELLS HOUSE PANEL TRUMP ADMIN MOVING TO DISMANTLE ‘FAILED’ $3T EDUCATION BUREAUCRACY

That distinction matters to students because recognition by a DOE-approved accreditor is generally necessary for schools to participate in federal student aid programs. NACCAS says it accredits approximately 1,300 institutions serving more than 120,000 students in cosmetology, beauty and related career programs.

DOE staff identified deficiencies with NACCAS but recommended continuing its federal recognition with restrictions, additional reporting and monitoring while it works to come into compliance.

The National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity, or NACIQI, took a harder line at its July meeting, voting 9-3 to recommend that the department deny NACCAS renewed recognition.

TRUMP ADMIN TIGHTENS VISE ON STUDENT AID FRAUD IN ‘GHOST STUDENT’ CRACKDOWN

The DOE has not made a final decision.

The Department of Education told Fox News Digital that accreditor recognition is reviewed every five years through a three-step process: DOE staff makes a recommendation; the independent bipartisan NACIQI makes its own recommendation; a senior department official makes the final judgment based on both.

"We will not comment on details as the process is ongoing," the DOE said.

For some students, the federal process has raised concerns about a source of funding they say they could not have attended beauty school without.

TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES

Aliyah Fernandez, a recent Hollywood Institute cosmetology graduate and mother who now works as an assistant in a salon, said federal aid made her education possible.

"I could not have afforded beauty school without federal financial aid," Fernandez told Fox News Digital. "It was because of that that I could attend at all."

Fernandez said she chose cosmetology in part because she wanted a career that would allow her to earn a living while remaining present in her daughter's life.

"I knew that if I worked full-time 9 to 5, I wouldn't barely have any time to see her grow up," Fernandez said. "I really just wanted to be there for her.

"I wanted an opportunity to financially support her and be present in her life at the same time," she added. "I wanted to have both."

I’M A UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT; TRUMP IS RIGHT TO MAKE COLLEGES DELIVER FOR STUDENTS

Blythe Fields, an expectant mother who is studying cosmetology while working in salons, said she previously paid for esthetician school herself and spent roughly two years saving her tips to continue her education.

"I paid out of pocket for esthetician school, and it made me go broke," Fields told Fox News Digital.

Fields said she now works during the day and attends school at night, describing her schedule as "literally 12-hour days."

She said federal financial aid allowed her to continue her education and that the flexibility of cosmetology will become even more important when her baby arrives.

"The first year is so important, and I need to be able to have that flexibility to raise a child," she said.

Fernandez and Fields both said they helped start a petition asking the DOE not to adopt NACIQI's recommendation outright. The petition calls instead for a monitored improvement period that would allow NACCAS to address the government's findings while maintaining recognition.

Fernandez said she understood why federal officials raised concerns about NACCAS but believed denying recognition would go too far.

FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING

"Having done the research myself, I can completely understand, you know, the side of the board," Fernandez said. "However, I do not think a full termination of accreditation is reasonable considering how many people rely on this."

Fields was more pointed when asked what she would tell Trump before his administration makes the final decision.

"I would ask him who cuts and colors his hair and how did they get there?" Fields said.

The disagreement over NACCAS centers on whether the deficiencies identified during its federal review warrant continued oversight or denial of recognition.

Education Department staff recommended that NACCAS be prohibited from accrediting additional institutions until it demonstrates compliance, complete corrective action within 12 months and submits additional reports to the department.

NACIQI instead recommended denial.

Zakiya Smith Ellis, a former Obama administration DOE official who serves on the advisory committee, made the motion to deny NACCAS renewed recognition.

Michael Poliakoff seconded the motion, which passed 9-3.

Smith Ellis argued during the July meeting that NACCAS had been given opportunities to address compliance problems and questioned whether giving it additional time would be sufficient. She also raised concerns about debt and earnings among students at NACCAS-accredited institutions.

Three committee members voted against denial, including Robert Eitel, who served in the DOE during Trump's first term.

Eitel argued that NACCAS should be required to correct its deficiencies rather than lose recognition and raised concerns about the potential consequences for the schools and students it oversees.

The proceeding also creates an unusual contrast with the accreditation practices Trump highlighted in his April executive order.

The order directed the DOE to investigate whether accreditors require schools to engage in unlawful discrimination, including through DEI-related standards. The federal findings at issue in the NACCAS proceeding concern compliance and oversight rather than an allegation that NACCAS imposes DEI requirements.

Smith Ellis, meanwhile, has publicly defended DEI policies and previously served as a senior DOE official during the Obama administration.

Fox News Digital asked Smith Ellis why she favored denying recognition rather than the corrective measures recommended by DOE staff and what she would say to students concerned about the potential consequences. Smith Ellis did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Fields told Fox News Digital she believes beauty careers can be overlooked in ways that other skilled trades are not. Asked whether she thought the same fight would be playing out around traditionally male-dominated trades such as plumbing or welding, she said she did not.

"I think it's because they're like male fields, like mainly men are involved in," Fields said. "They don't think about that. They just think, ‘Oh, they went to hair school. It's easy.’"

For Fields, however, the training will give her the career she hopes will allow her to earn a living while raising her child.

The White House, NACCAS, and the Hollywood Institute of Beauty did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

item.title: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announces distribution of more than 7 million free eggs statewide
item.description: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced 1.7 million free eggs have reached Texas food banks, with 5.3 million more on the way from a settlement.
item.content:encoded:
More than 1.7 million free eggs have already been delivered to Texas food banks, with another 5.3 million slated to arrive in the coming weeks as part of an antitrust settlement with three major egg producers, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced Tuesday.

The statewide distribution stems from settlements reached in June with Cal-Maine Foods, Centrum/Versova and Hickman's Egg Ranch, resolving antitrust claims brought by the Trump administration's Department of Justice and a coalition of state attorneys general over allegations the companies conspired to inflate egg prices between 2022 and 2025.

Under the agreements, the companies will donate more than 7 million eggs to Texas food banks and pay a combined $3.3 million to participating states.

"After securing 7 million eggs for the people of Texas, I am excited to announce that Texans will now have an opportunity to receive cartons of free eggs in communities across the state," Paxton said. "I will continue to help our families put food on the table and do everything within my power to lower prices and help Texans who are struggling to make ends meet."

TRUMP-LINKED MAGA INC POURS $10M INTO KEN PAXTON'S TEXAS SENATE RACE AGAINST JAMES TALARICO

The distributions are being coordinated with Feeding Texas, the state's largest hunger-relief organization. Seventeen food banks are participating in the effort.

The Houston Food Bank is expected to receive the largest allocation of 1,544,400 eggs, followed by the North Texas Food Bank in Plano and the Tarrant Area Food Bank in Fort Worth, which will each receive 842,400 eggs. Other participating food banks are located across the state, including Austin, San Antonio, Tyler, Corpus Christi, El Paso, Laredo, Odessa, Pharr, Beaumont, Amarillo, Lubbock, Victoria, Abilene and Wichita Falls.

AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE

It was not immediately clear when individual food banks would begin distributing the eggs to Texans or whether eligibility requirements would vary by location.

A spokesperson for Feeding Texas did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on distribution timing and how Texans can receive the eggs. Fox News Digital also reached out to Cal-Maine Foods for comment on the settlement and the statewide donation effort.

item.title: Stephen A Smith blasts SEC for threats to kick LSU out of the conference: 'Sit your a-- down'
item.description: Lane Kiffin's bold move to bring NFL-cut players back to LSU through the transfer portal sparked SEC threats to expel the Tigers from the conference.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 college football season is off to a surprisingly controversial start. Out of nowhere, the Western Michigan-Michigan game became one of the most contentious finishes in recent memory, with replay review adding an additional second to the fourth quarter after the game had seemingly ended.

That sparked a formal appeal from the MAC to the FBS Oversight Committee and the College Football Playoff to recognize the Broncos as the official winners, due to improper replay review procedures.

Then there’s the human element: new LSU head coach Lane Kiffin. Kiffin drew criticism for his lengthy, drawn-out decision-making process after LSU offered him the job in Baton Rouge. His eventual decision to leave Ole Miss before the College Football Playoff made him public enemy No. 1 in Oxford. Somehow, the questions surrounding Kiffin have only deepened over time.

LSU’S LANE KIFFIN FIRES BACK AT NFL RETURNEE BACKLASH: BLAME THE NCAA, NOT US FOR RECRUITING PRO ATHLETES

Kiffin set about reshaping the Tigers' program through the transfer portal, then apparently had an even more unique and extreme idea: bring players who had signed with NFL teams but failed to make the regular season roster back to college football. Obviously designed to give LSU an advantage by adding more physically advanced and developed players, that tactic was immediately disparaged by opposing coaches, NFL coaches and, more importantly, the SEC itself.

A war of words and policies ensued with multiple conferences, including the SEC, immediately passing a policy to prevent "pro" players returning to the collegiate ranks. LSU fought back, even winning an injunction to allow two players, Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, to confirm their eligibility.

That led to some extreme measures being discussed, including reports this week that the SEC was prepared to vote imminently to expel LSU from the conference entirely. As shocking and extreme as that sounds, it's clear that the SEC wanted to ensure that their commitment to "amateur" athletics remained unblemished.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Some supported the potential vote as a punishment for Kiffin and the Tigers program pushing the limits of eligibility. And further SEC filings implied that the athletic director had little control of the football team, with Kiffin alone running the ship.

But Stephen A. Smith, apparently, strongly disagrees, saying that just signing a contract in the NFL does not make you an "NFL player."

"Just because you enter a draft — if you haven’t signed a contract with the NFL team, you are not an NFL player," he said during a recent episode of "First Take" on ESPN. "If you haven’t been on a practice field, if you haven’t competed against NFL players, you are not an NFL player. You should be able to go back to college. That’s the one thing that I do feel."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Smith wasn't done there, saying that LSU being pushed into independence may actually help the program.

"And oh, by the way, Notre Dame, and we got love for Notre Dame, they’re an independent," he added. "LSU, you wanna throw them out the SEC? Go ahead and do it. Watch, they ain’t gonna lose. They’ll be just fine…Could you imagine Lane Kiffin as an independent? Out there in the open market for the LSU brand? Please, they’ll get paid…The SEC, sit your a-- down! Sit your a-- down!"

The Tigers seemingly backed down from their plan this week, signaling by adding two other players to their roster that they wouldn't bring in those former "NFL" players. But Smith seems to have a different perspective on this than most fans or rival administrators and coaches. Once you leave college and sign with an NFL team, that's it. You're done. That's how it's always been, and changing it now opens up a can of worms.

Would a player who’s, say, only made the practice squad be considered an "NFL player" in Smith’s view? Or would they still be eligible to return? What about another who is on an active roster, but never enters a game? Or someone who plays just one game before getting hurt? Defining who and who isn't a professional becomes a game of Whac-A-Mole that shouldn't be necessary.

Stephen A., though, clearly doesn't see it that way. He's wrong.

item.title: ‘Kirkiversary’ Charlie Kirk look-alike contest advertised at University of South Carolina to mark killing
item.description: Anonymous social media posts promoted a Charlie Kirk look-alike contest called "Kirkiversary" at the University of South Carolina ahead of the Sept. 10 anniversary of Kirk's killing.
item.content:encoded:
An apparent Charlie Kirk look-alike contest called "Kirkiversary" is being advertised at the University of South Carolina for Sept. 10, the anniversary of the conservative activist’s assassination.

A screenshot of an anonymous Yik Yak post circulating on social media advertises a "Charlie Kirk look-alike contest" on Greene Street outside USC’s Russell House at 7 p.m., offering a $50 prize and telling prospective participants, "Be there or be square."

Kirk, the 31-year-old founder of Turning Point USA, was assassinated Sept. 10, 2025, while speaking at Utah Valley University during his "American Comeback Tour."

It was not immediately clear who created the post or organized the apparent event, whether those involved are USC students or not.

ERIKA KIRK PENS ESSAY ON GRIEF AS READERS GAIN INSIGHTS INTO WRENCHING PAST YEAR

Libs of TikTok amplified the post Wednesday, characterizing the contest as an event organized by students to celebrate Kirk’s assassination and calling it "demonic." The underlying Yik Yak post reviewed by Fox News Digital referred to the event as "Kirkiversary" but does not explicitly state that its purpose is to celebrate Kirk’s killing.

The University of South Carolina replied to the Libs of TikTok post saying, "We have no record of any registered student organization planning such an event. No university resources will be used to support this. DM us if you’d like a contact here that can help verify claims like this ahead of posting."

INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES

Students at Georgetown University also allegedly planned a Kirk "lookalike contest" for the anniversary of his assassination, with the event drawing thousands of upvotes at the elite Washington, D.C., campus, according to screenshots shared with Fox News Digital by the school’s Turning Point USA chapter.

The Sept. 10 event was promoted on Fizz, an anonymous social media platform popular with Georgetown students, where the initial announcement received more than 2,200 upvotes. Georgetown's undergraduate population is roughly 6,000.

item.title: Jet plunges 27,000 feet in 10 minutes as oxygen masks suddenly drop aboard flight
item.description: Delta Air Lines Flight 2311 experienced a scary emergency when the plane descended roughly 27,000 feet in about 10 minutes because of a pressurization issue.
item.content:encoded:
Travelers aboard a recent Delta Air Lines flight faced a midair scare when oxygen masks suddenly dropped in the passenger cabin.

A pressurization issue occurred aboard Delta Flight 2311 on Sept. 6, prompting the crew to bring the plane to a lower altitude and divert to Las Vegas, a Delta spokesperson told Fox News Digital. 

The flight was carrying 174 passengers and six crew members.

'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS

"As safety comes before everything else at Delta, the flight crew of Delta flight 2311 LAX-SLC followed their training and procedures to safely bring the aircraft to optimal altitude when an unexpected pressurization issue occurred," the spokesperson said.

The flight, which was traveling from Los Angeles to Salt Lake City, descended roughly 27,000 feet in about 10 minutes as oxygen masks deployed in the cabin, according to reports.

News of the rapid descent could be heard in communications between the pilots and air traffic control.

"Delta 2311 currently [in] rapid descent. We'd like to get down to 9,000, and we're direct [to] Las Vegas," a pilot said in an air traffic control recording, according to reports.

When an air traffic controller asked, "Is the oxygen deployed?" the pilot responded, "Affirmative."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The aircraft landed safely at Harry Reid International Airport in Vegas, where passengers exited normally, according to Delta.

Delta arranged for another aircraft so that passengers could continue on with their journey.

"Delta sincerely apologizes to our customers for their experience and thanks our flight crews and other support teams on the ground for their professionalism," the spokesperson said.

Matthew "Whiz" Buckley of Florida, a retired U.S. Navy F/A-18 fighter pilot with nearly 40 years of flying experience, said such a pressurization occurrence "is an extremely rare issue" in the United States. 

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

In a case such as the Delta one, he told Fox News Digital pilots in this scenario would need "to land as soon as practical — meaning, what's the closest airfield with a nice, long, suitable runway where we can get this thing on the ground safely."

The incident drew attention online. A passenger aboard the flight talked about the chaos inside the cabin.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The scariest part wasn't even the descent — it was not knowing what was going on," the passenger wrote on Reddit. "Flight attendants were trying to make announcements with their masks on, and it was almost impossible to hear them."

The passenger was reportedly asleep when a fiancé said something about what was going on.

"It took me another second of 'Is this real or am I dreaming?' before getting our masks on," the traveler wrote.

"I was frantically trying to see if I could get on WiFi because I didn't know if I was going to have to be sending out 'I love you' texts," the person added.

Other travelers responded to the post by sharing their own experiences with oxygen masks and rapid descents.

One Reddit user recalled a previous Delta flight that descended from about 34,000 feet to 10,000 feet while passengers wore oxygen masks.

"The several minutes of rapid descent ... [were] pretty jarring until the captain finally came on the mic once we were at a safe altitude," the commenter wrote, adding that passengers remained quiet and focused on breathing through their masks.

item.title: LSU President Wade Rousse ends Lane Kiffin’s SEC showdown, but there is still relationships to mend
item.description: A Birmingham Alabama federal court hearing was delayed after LSU backed down and finalized its roster without former pro-athletes Wright or Harris.
item.content:encoded:
The ongoing battle between the SEC and LSU was set to be heard in a courtroom on Wednesday afternoon in Birmingham, Alabama.

But, just 10 minutes before the scheduled hearing in federal court over whether the SEC would be granted the power to enforce its rules pertaining to former pro-athletes returning to college athletics, lawyers for both sides met inside the chambers of the presiding judge to discuss a resolution.

A decision was made to continue the case to a later date, if needed and cooler heads looked to prevail out of Baton Rouge.

LSU HOLDS OFF ON ADDING PLAYERS WITH NFL TIES AS SEC LAWSUIT LOOMS OVER PROGRAM, LANE KIFFIN

Call it 'waving the white flag' or however you'd prefer, but LSU has backed down from its stance on adding players to their roster that have professional experience in some form or fashion.

One night before the SEC was scheduled to ask a federal judge in Alabama for a temporary restraining order, LSU has finalized its roster for the upcoming season.

That doesn’t mean the SEC is not going to be meeting on Thursday regarding potential punishments for the LSU Tigers, though.

JUDGE GRANTS INJUNCTION AGAINST NCAA, SEC, ALLOWING ATHLETES WITH NFL TIES ELIGIBLE TO PLAY FOR LSU, OTHERS

After nearly three weeks of court appearances involving multiple athletes in the Louisiana case, including former Ole Miss players Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, the Tigers decided not to add either player to its roster at any point this season.

The decision comes after both sides were embroiled in a fight that saw SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey make an appearance in a Louisiana district court to testify on behalf of his conference. During those proceedings, the lawsuit filed by the SEC was brought up during questioning.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

"Did you authorize the SEC to sue LSU and coach Lane Kiffin?" attorney Tony Clayton asked Sankey.

When asked why the conference took that step, Sankey pointed to the authority of the presidents and chancellors he represents.

"We established our First Amendment right for freedom of association, so that our conference can make decisions and our members can make decisions about membership," Sankey said.

At that point, all options were on the table of how to move forward.

Judging by the decision of LSU on Tuesday night into Wednesday morning, it was starting to become much clearer that the Tigers had finally backed down.

The back-and-forth between all parties involved came to a head last Friday, when SEC presidents and chancellors had seen enough.

At one point, a number of school officials were prepared to punish the school, with the topic of expulsion being brought up numerous times. While this never felt like a realistic option, the threat weighed heavy on the minds of folks around Baton Rouge.

In a letter sent to SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey on Wednesday morning, and obtained by OutKick, LSU President Wade Rousse wanted to make it clear that the Tigers were going to comply with conference rules and not roster any of the athletes who would have been eligible under a court injunction.

"On the afternoon of September 4, 2026, I called and provided you with advance notice that LSU would not place Dae'Quan Wright or Zxavian Harris on the football roster," President Rousse explained. "This was confirmed when LSU submitted its roster later that evening. On September 8, 2026, LSU filled its two remaining roster spots with eligible student-athletes. The roster is now locked for the season.

"LSU complied with SEC rules. The issue is now mute."

In terms of the meeting that was scheduled for Thursday between SEC presidents and chancellors to vote on what type of punishments to levy against LSU for this whole saga, President Rousse tried to make it clear that there would not be a challenge from the school, but the issue was now finalized.

"Also on September 8, 2026, I received notice of the special President's and Chancellor's meeting scheduled for tomorrow, September 10, 2026. At no point has LSU ever threatened to upset that meeting," President Rousse explained. "But to be clear, LSU will not challenge, disrupt or seek to cancel or postpone this meeting.

"This issue is also moot."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

All of this could have transpired weeks ago, when the SEC released its guidelines pertaining to rules on professional athletes returning to college sports.

But, it looked as though the Tigers wanted to challenge the conference on its stance. While LSU was never actually named in the lawsuit pertaining to the athletes in a Baton Rouge court, they were certainly in the news.

Thanks to statements from Governor Jeff Landry, along with Attorney General Liz Murrill showing up to the courthouse wearing a purple blouse and exclaiming 'Go Tigers' before entering the courthouse, it was obvious that while LSU officials were not present, government officials were trying to speak on their behalf.

In reality, that's where this whole ordeal turned into a political sideshow that felt more like propaganda than the actual athletes involved in the case.

Now, six days after the hearing inside a Baton Rouge court, the LSU Tigers are finally doing us all a favor and moving on from this nonsense that has diverted attention away from the college football season.

And no, this does not mean we are done hearing about athletes from LSU being involved in legal arguments, as the school still has to make a decision on basketball player RJ Luis.

We will see what the SEC decides to do on Thursday, but I think it's pretty clear that it was time for this circus to come to an end.

item.title: Chinese nationals accused of smuggling synthetic drugs into US prisons on drug-soaked paper
item.description: Two Chinese nationals allegedly shipped synthetic opioids and cannabinoids to U.S. co-defendants who soaked paper with the drugs and mailed them to inmates.
item.content:encoded:
Two Chinese nationals were arrested in China after allegedly supplying synthetic drugs that prosecutors say were imported into the United States and later distributed to inmates at federal and state prisons nationwide.

Lisa Xing, 36, and Zhanwen Song, 38, were charged in a superseding federal indictment in the Eastern District of Texas with drug trafficking and money laundering offenses tied to an alleged scheme that allegedly supplied synthetic opioids, cannabinoids and other drugs from China for distribution in U.S. correctional facilities.

FBI Director Kash Patel touted the case in a post on X, writing that the defendants allegedly trafficked "dangerous synthetic drugs from China into the United States — including smuggling them into our prison systems."

"This FBI and our Homeland Security Task Force partners will keep finding and disrupting these networks wherever they operate," Patel wrote. "Great work by @FBIDallas and our law enforcement partners."

EXCLUSIVE: FENTANYL DEATHS PLUNGE 22% AS TRUMP WHITE HOUSE TOUTS CRACKDOWN ON DEADLY DRUG CRISIS

According to prosecutors, Xing and Song shipped synthetic drugs to co-defendants Adell Willis of Texas and Judy Ly of Michigan, who allegedly dissolved the drugs into liquid, soaked sheets of paper in the mixture and mailed them to inmates in federal and state prisons across the country.

Willis and Ly were indicted in May on charges, including conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

FEDERAL INMATES MAY SOON GET TABLETS WITH MESSAGING CAPABILITIES AS BUREAU OF PRISONS MAKES MODERNIZATION PUSH

"The indictment alleges that a China-based supplier and a domestic distributor worked together to bring deadly synthetic drugs into the United States for distribution across the country," U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs said.

The Justice Department said China's Ministry of Public Security arrested Xing, Song and 19 additional alleged co-conspirators, seized 475 kilograms of synthetic cannabinoids and shut down four illicit manufacturing sites. Officials said the investigation was coordinated through an FBI-Chinese Ministry of Public Security counternarcotics working group established earlier this year.

If convicted, each defendant faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years in prison and up to life behind bars.

item.title: Local GOP leader slams $50K taxpayer 'slush fund' for families of detained, deported immigrant breadwinners
item.description: A Virginia GOP leader calls Arlington County's $50,000 in taxpayer-funded grants for families of deported illegal immigrants a "slush fund."
item.content:encoded:
A Virginia GOP leader is pushing back against a new county program to provide taxpayer-funded grants to the families of illegal immigrants whose primary wage earner was detained or deported by federal immigration authorities.

Arlington County, which sits across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C., endorsed a plan on Sept. 2 to appropriate $50,000 for the social safety net program. 

Under the terms of the project, the funds would be given to the nonprofit Arlington Thrive, which would provide up to $2,000 to the families to cover basic needs.

"This flies in the face of the Trump administration policy, and it is a detriment to taxpayers of Arlington, tens of thousands of whom are conservative and Republican and oppose this policy," Matthew Hurtt, chairman of the Arlington County GOP, told Fox News Digital.

'ALIEN HARBORING' ACCUSATIONS FLY AS DC-AREA COUNTY SPENDS TAXPAYER FUNDS TO BLUNT ICE

Hurtt described the money as a "slush fund" designed to further oppose the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration. He noted that since Arlington Thrive is a nonprofit, it is exempt from transparency protocols that normally apply to government agencies.

The County Board praised the program at a special meeting, where it voted 4-0 with one member absent.

FIRST ON FOX: ICE QUIETLY ARRESTS JAW-DROPPING NUMBER OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS IN MASSIVE DC AREA OPERATION

"We stand with our immigrant families, and we will not stop doing so," Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said. "We are valuing the families of those that have been displaced and removed."

The move follows a recent law enforcement operation in which more than 1,300 illegal immigrants were arrested over a two-week period in the Washington, D.C., and Virginia area.

In January, as part of the county's opposition to immigration enforcement, de Ferranti urged residents to report sightings of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to county authorities.

Arlington County, as well as other counties in Northern Virginia, have for years tried to subvert the Trump administration's efforts to fight illegal immigration through various sanctuary policies, Hurtt said.

DOJ ACCUSES MARYLAND OF 'ACTIVE AND DELIBERATE EFFORT' TO PREVENT DEPORTATIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS: LAWSUIT

"Arlington County, Fairfax County and other Northern Virginia counties are completely run by far-left activists who love this kind of program," he said. "They have, for years, since President Trump's first administration, sought to be the first line of defense against the orange man.

"So, if something happens in Washington that is supported by Republicans, the county board in Arlington and Fairfax does exactly the opposite."

Meanwhile, Hurtt said, county leaders have pushed for voters to support bond measures for critical services, which are covered by additional taxes.

"Every single election cycle, the Arlington County board puts hundreds of millions of dollars on the ballot in the form of bond issues for basic services — school improvements, road construction and other projects that they deem necessary," he said.

"What that tells voters is that they aren't prioritizing those projects, projects that they bond out and borrow dollar after dollar, but they're prioritizing these far-left projects like a slush fund for illegal aliens."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Arlington County Democrats and the County Board for comment.

item.title: Raiders star Brock Bowers shockingly undergoes meniscus trim surgery as fantasy managers fume ahead of Week 1
item.description: Las Vegas Raiders star Brock Bowers underwent meniscus surgery in Dallas and is expected to miss a game or two, blindsiding fantasy football managers.
item.content:encoded:
News from the Las Vegas Raiders has fantasy football managers across the country fuming, especially those who made sure to draft close to the start of the NFL season.

Star tight end Brock Bowers underwent a meniscus trim on Tuesday in Dallas, and he’s now expected to miss "a game or two," according to ESPN.

This is a tremendous blow to the Raiders’ new-look offense under head coach Klint Kubiak, as Bowers, who dealt with lingering knee issues last season, was expected to be Kirk Cousins’ top target entering the new campaign.

The report added that Bowers was banged up "a little in camp," and he had the injury diagnosed last week. Surgery was scheduled and Dr. Daniel Cooper operated on Bowers, who will now hope to return in Week 3, though the "game or two" timeline can always vary depending on the player.

While Bowers isn’t expected to miss significant time at the moment, an interesting part of the report is the fact the Raiders knew since last week, but it was never mentioned.

Of course, teams don’t care how fantasy football lineups are impacted throughout the season. But for a league that has roughly 40 million Americans playing fantasy football annually, which relies heavily on disclosed injuries in terms of drafting and lineups being placed, Bowers’ injury is shocking those who own him as the 2026 season kicks off in Seattle on Wednesday night.

Bowers is also a top draft choice for many in fantasy football considering the volume he receives for the Raiders as well as his outstanding rookie campaign, where he totaled 1,194 yards on 112 receptions with five touchdowns.

Had fantasy managers known about Bowers’ injury, skepticism about taking him with such a high pick would’ve likely entered the minds of many.

To make matters worse, Kubiak was asked during a press conference just hours before news broke about Bowers' injury if he and Maxx Crosby, who dealt with injuries last season and wasn't used much during preseason contests, would be available on Sunday.

"We’re expecting to have all our guys ready for Sunday," Kubiak replied.

So, either Kubiak was blatantly lying about Bowers' condition, or he didn't know that one of his best players could be missing time after getting surgery on Tuesday in Dallas. Not the best way to start off the new year.

Bowers was unable to see his rookie-year production in 2025 due to his PCL sprain and bone bruiser that pestered him since Week 1’s victory over the New England Patriots. He missed several weeks, ultimately playing in 12 games (eight starts) before being placed on the season-ending injured reserve for the final two weeks of the year.

As NFL reporter Ari Meirov pointed out on X, a meniscus trim usually takes four-to-six weeks to recover from, but the Raiders appear optimistic Bowers will be back before then. A full meniscus repair is a season-ending injury — Minnesota Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy missed his entire rookie campaign due to that exact injury.

In the meantime, fantasy managers could be quick to pick up Michael Mayer, the Raiders’ second tight end, off waivers if he’s available. Mayer was always going to work within this offense, as Bowers can be placed anywhere on the line of scrimmage due to his route-running abilities for a tight end.

Now, Cousins will need to rely on Mayer to pick up the slack against the Miami Dolphins, whom they host at Allegiant Stadium on Sunday.
